## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no results yet, and scores stay hidden for the whole search. Each trial will only tell us whether it trained or failed, so each candidate should be a well-reasoned best guess rather than a clean one-variable test. The starting network encodes each column with 1x1 convolutions and passes it through two 3x3 convolutions, which see a 5x5 area, then scores each brick type by pooling over its footprint. With 131k steps the run gets only about 32 PPO updates, so sample efficiency and update frequency probably matter most. The structural problem is that the network must work out the landing layer (the highest build cell under the footprint) and check the target at that layer. Proposals: (1) the starting network with a recipe that updates more often on fresher data; (2) a per-layer head that scores each placement at every layer and uses a learned soft gate to pick the landing layer; (3) a deeper trunk that adds a global summary to every cell, plus a recipe tweak.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials trained without errors, but scores are hidden, so the results give no evidence about which ideas help. Every proposal therefore rests on prior reasoning about the task. In the drop rule, a brick's landing layer depends on the column heights under its footprint, and placement order matters wherever a design has an overhang. Round 1 tested three ideas: heads that model layers directly, a deeper trunk with whole-board context, and fresher on-policy data. With 6 trials left, this round makes one recipe-only change to the r1c3 trunk: 2 PPO epochs instead of 3, which buys about 180k samples. It also tests a new idea, self-attention across all cells, so each placement score can depend on the whole board's progress and ordering. Finally, it combines the two structural ideas from round 1: the r1c3 trunk with the r1c2 layer-gated head. All three stay under 2x the starting network's compute.

### Round 3
Scores are hidden, so I can't rank the six trials. All of them trained without errors, including the 1.8x-cost ones, so the time limit isn't binding at this scale. The candidates below rest on how the task works, not on measured results. A placement is correct only if every footprint cell is missing in the target at the landing layer, which is the highest build cell under the footprint, and if it doesn't seal target cells below. The layer-gated head (r1c2, r2c3) fits this rule, but its per-layer input only sees the layer directly above and below. It can't tell whether a column is empty all the way up, or whether target cells further down are still unfilled. A legal fix is to give each layer the whole column, re-indexed relative to that layer, using only padding and slicing. A learned layer can then work out what lands where and what would get sealed. All three candidates use this input and vary the trunk, the sample count and the spatial context inside the head.

### Round 4
No scores are visible, so I can't rank the trials. All 9 trials trained without errors, so files of this kind stay within the time limit. Each trial ran 2 seeds, and seed luck alone can decide whether a run succeeds or fails. This is the last round, so the aim is to spread three plausible bets rather than run a clean ablation. The idea that best matches the task is the relative-column, layer-gated head (r3c1–r3c3). It follows the drop rule: for each candidate landing layer, it looks at whether there is support below and space above. It also checks what the target still needs above and below. The open questions are:
- whether a lean trunk, which buys more samples, beats a deep one;
- whether spatial mixing inside each layer helps;
- whether summing features over the footprint with a learned convolution beats fixed pooling;
- whether a longer horizon helps the agent learn from the bonus it gets only for an exact build.
Each candidate below tests one of these, starting from a relative-column design.
